Why Did Apple Fall To The Ground: Evaluating Curiosity In Large Language Model

Haoyu Wang    Sihang Jiang    Yuyan Chen    Yitong Wang    Yanghua Xiao Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University Email: wanghy24@m.fudan.edu.cn
Abstract

Curiosity serves as a pivotal conduit for human beings to discover and learn new knowledge. Recent advancements of large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing have sparked discussions regarding whether these models possess capability of curiosity-driven learning akin to humans. In this paper, starting from the human curiosity assessment questionnaire Five-Dimensional Curiosity scale Revised (5DCR), we design a comprehensive evaluation framework that covers dimensions such as Information Seeking, Thrill Seeking, and Social Curiosity to assess the extent of curiosity exhibited by LLMs. The results demonstrate that LLMs exhibit a stronger thirst for knowledge than humans but still tend to make conservative choices when faced with uncertain environments. We further investigated the relationship between curiosity and thinking of LLMs, confirming that curious behaviors can enhance the model’s reasoning and active learning abilities. These findings suggest that LLMs have the potential to exhibit curiosity similar to that of humans, providing experimental support for the future development of learning capabilities and innovative research in LLMs.

1 Introduction

Curiosity, a significant and intrinsic trait of human that emerges when facing new environments, serves as a crucial conduit for the discovery of knowledge Berlyne et al. (1954); Loewenstein (1994). Throughout human history, numerous scientific breakthroughs have been spurred by curiosity, as exemplified by Sir Isaac Newton’s discovery of universal gravitation from observing a falling apple. It is the pursuit of information driven by curiosity that motivates humans to continuously pose new questions, explore new environments, thereby acquiring new knowledge Silvia (2012).

In recent years, large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT Floridi and Chiriatti (2020) have demonstrated powerful capabilities in language understanding Wang et al. (2023) and world knowledge Zhao et al. (2024). However, unlike humans who acquire knowledge through questioning and exploration, LLMs are primarily trained via next-token prediction on corpora, which may lead to a limited performance ceiling Burns et al. (2023). While recent reinforcement learning (RL) Kaelbling et al. (1996) techniques such as GRPO Shao et al. (2024) have enabled LLMs to exhibit deep thinking in specific domains like mathematics and coding, their general-domain comprehension and learning abilities have not seen comparable improvements.

To address these limitations, recent research has begun to leverage curiosity to guide models in autonomous exploration, thereby enabling generalization to broader domains such as multi-turn dialogue and creative text generation Sun et al. (2025); Wan et al. (2025); Dai et al. (2025). The curiosity of LLMs for active learning Settles (2009) has emerged as an issue warranting attention. However, as the foundation of such approaches, whether LLMs can exhibit curious behaviors akin to humans remains insufficiently and systematically evaluated. Moreover, existing curiosity-driven RL methods still rely on the actor-critic framework and well-defined reward functions, making it difficult to disentangle whether performance improvements stem from enhanced external supervision signals or the model’s intrinsic curiosity. To this end, it is necessary to evaluate the curiosity exhibited by LLMs.

To comprehensively evaluate and analysis the curiosity of LLMs, this paper designs assessments to explore the following research questions: RQ1 Can LLMs exhibit curiosity similar to that of humans? RQ2 How does curiosity in LLMs differ from human curiosity? RQ3 Can intrinsic curiosity in LLMs enhance reasoning and active learning abilities?

An overview of our curiosity evaluation is illustrated in Figure 1. A) Inspired by the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR) Kashdan et al. (2020), we classify curiosity into three categories: Information Seeking, Thrill Seeking and Social Curiosity. B) We prompt LLMs with 5DCR questionnaires to obtain preliminary results for curiosity assessment. C) We conduct curious behavior studies corresponding to each of the three dimensions outlined in part A, verifying the model’s curiosity in actual scenarios. D) We design a curiosity-driven questioning and thinking pipeline for LLMs to investigate the relationship between curiosity and learning in LLMs.

Our findings indicate that:

  1. 1.

    LLMs generally exhibit stronger curiosity than humans. Results of the curiosity questionnaire and behavioral experiment both indicate that LLMs have the ability to exhibit curious behaviors, providing experimental support for curiosity-driven active learning in LLMs.

  2. 2.

    LLMs exhibit a strong curiosity towards knowledge, yet maintain a cautious stance regarding the thrill and pressure that curiosity may engender.. LLMs demonstrate a greater desire for learning knowledge and new information, but tend to make conservative choices rather than pursuing stimulation as humans.

  3. 3.

    Curious questioning and thinking enhance the active learning ability of LLMs. By asking more auxiliary questions, models can reduce the premature conclusions and meaningless repetitive thinking, and can generate some key inspirations.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that systematically evaluates curiosity in LLMs. In conclusion, our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose a systematic evaluation for curiosity in LLMs. This evaluation encompasses questionnaire-based and behavioral assessment for curiosity, covering three dimensions, thereby providing a comprehensive quantification of curiosity in LLMs.

  • •

    We evaluate the curiosity of mainstream LLMs and compare with those of humans. Results indicate that while LLMs exhibit a stronger desire for knowledge than humans, they are more restrained in thrill seeking.

  • •

    We demonstrate the correlation between curiosity and active learning ability of LLMs. This indicates that curiosity-driven learning is a new paradigm for enhancing the capabilities of models.

2 Related Work

2.1 Evaluation of Curiosity

Research and evaluation of human curiosity originated from Berlyne’s four-dimensional model of curiosity Berlyne (1966), which categorizes curiosity into perceptual curiosity, cognitive curiosity, trait curiosity, and state curiosity. As definitions and descriptions of curiosity became more refined, the assessment of curiosity shifted towards scale-based methods, with significant contributions from the Perceptual Curiosity Scale (PC) Collins et al. (2004) and the Curiosity and Exploration Inventory (CEI) Kashdan et al. (2009). The most recent and authoritative scale in psychological research for measuring curiosity is the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR) Kashdan et al. (2020), which based on a six-dimensional model of curiosity and refines the wording of certain items. Consequently, this paper adopts the 5DCR and its dimensional definitions of curiosity as the theoretical reference.

2.2 Curiosity in Language Model

The theory of curiosity has been widely applied in natural language processing research, with its initial adoption in question generation and evaluation. Scialom et al. assessed the degree of curiosity in questions within the SQuAD dataset based on BLEU scores and perplexity Scialom and Staiano (2020). Gao et al. designed multiple types of curious questions, which were annotated by humans, and demonstrated that curious questions contribute to improvements in the grammaticality, semantics, and relevance of generated texts Gao et al. (2022) . Javaji et al. collected questions posed by LLMs in disciplines such as physics and chemistry, evaluating the models’ abilities to generate curious questions Javaji and Zhu (2024). In recent years, curiosity-driven RL algorithms have also achieved notable success. CD-RLHF enhances the diversity of texts generated by LLMs by rewarding the generation of less common tokens Sun et al. (2025). CURIO incorporates a user model to integrate curiosity-based intrinsic reward mechanisms into multi-turn dialogue training, thereby improving the personalization of LLMs in dialogue recommendation tasks Wan et al. (2025). CDE formalizes curiosity through signals from both the actor and critic, which helps to mitigate premature convergence and collapse in the reasoning processes of models Dai et al. (2025).

3 Method

In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of how to evaluate the curiosity of LLMs through questionnaires and behavioral experiments, and how to enhance the active learning ability of LLMs through curiosity-driven questioning. The framework is shown in Fig. 1.

3.1 Curiosity Questionnaire Study

Initially, adhering to established methodologies for assessing human curiosity, we prompt LLMs to self-evaluate their level of curiosity using the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale Revised (5DCR) Kashdan et al. (2020). The 5DCR conceptualizes human curiosity across three overarching dimensions—Information Seeking, Thrill Seeking, and Social Curiosity—which are further delineated into six specific subdimensions: Joyous Exploration (JE), Deprivation Sensitivity (DS), Stress Tolerance (ST), Thrill Seeking (TS), Overt Social Curiosity (OSC), and Covert Social Curiosity (CSC). The scale consists of 24 items, with each subdimension represented by four statements. For each statement, the model is prompted to rate the extent to which the statement reflects its own disposition using a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Detailed experimental settings are provided in the Appendix.

In addition to essential metrics such as mean and variance, we also considered multiple other metrics during analyzing to further investigate the differences between model and human performance, as well as the validity of the model’s self-reports. Cohen’s d Diener (2010) is particularly utilized to quantify the standardized difference between the means of models and humans, which is defined as:

d=X¯1−X¯2sd=\frac{\bar{X}_{1}-\bar{X}_{2}}{s}

where X¯1\bar{X}_{1} and X¯2\bar{X}_{2} denote the means of samples, while ss represents the pooled standard deviation of these samples. Furthermore, McDonald’s Omega Coefficient Bonniga and Saraswathi (2020) describes the proportion of total variance attributed to common variance among observed variables, serving as an indicator of internal reliability for questionnaire. The formula for McDonald’s Omega can be delineated based on the outcomes of Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) Harrington (2009):

ω=(∑i=1kλi)2(∑i=1kλi)2+∑i=1kθi\omega=\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i})^{2}}{(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i})^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\theta_{i}}

where kk signifies the number of items in the questionnaire, λi\lambda_{i} indicates the standardized CFA factor loading of the iith item on the common factor, reflecting the degree of correlation between the item and the latent variable. θi\theta_{i} denotes the error variance of the ii-th item, embodying the portion of variance not explained by the latent variable.

In summary, a higher value of dd reflects a more pronounced divergence between model and human performance, while a higher ω\omega value indicates greater internal consistency and reliability in the model’s questionnaire responses.

3.2 Curious Behavior Study

The responses of LLMs to questionnaires are not entirely reliable, as they are influenced by various factors such as persona hallucination, questionnaire language and scale Han et al. (2025). Consequently, from the three dimensions of curiosity, we adopt psychology behavioral experiments originally designed for humans, aiming to verify the questionnaire results by observing the actual behavior of models in curiosity-related scenarios, as shown in Fig. 4.

Curiosity-Driven Information Seeking We reference the missing-letter game designed by Singh et al. Singh and Manjaly (2021) to evaluate Curiosity-Driven Information Seeking, as shown in Fig. 2a. The model is prompted to complete a series of incomplete words. After completing, the model can choose whether to view the answer. The choice of the model demonstrates its curiosity about unknown information. We categorize the model’s inclination to view answers into four levels, enabling the quantification of the model’s curiosity intensity for information seeking and the comparison with experimental data of human participants.

Curiosity-Driven Thrill Seeking We reference the underwater game designed by Jirout et al. Jirout and Klahr (2012) to evaluate Curiosity-Driven Thrill Seeking, as shown in Fig. 2b. The LLM is informed that it is inside a submarine and can observe fishes throughout windows. Two windows are available for selection, each representing different degrees of uncertainty: a window with low uncertainty allows the model to know exactly what kind of fish will be seen, while a high-uncertainty window means the observed fish are random. By analyzing the difference in uncertainty between the windows, we calculate the LLMs’ curiosity extent, and compare them with the experimental data of human. A higher curiosity extent indicates that the model is more likely to open the window corresponding to high-uncertainty options, whereas a lower curiosity extent implies the model prefers to observe confirmed fish.

Social Curiosity We adapt the experiment designed by Hartung et al. Hartung and Renner (2011) to evaluate Social Curiosity, as shown in Fig. 2c. The model engages in ten rounds of daily conversation with a stranger of random personality (role-played by GPT-4o Achiam et al. (2023)). The frequency of questions posed by the model during these conversations reflects its curiosity about others’ information in social scenarios.

3.3 Curiosity-Driven Learning

After evaluating the curiosity extent of LLMs across three dimensions, we explore the relationship between curiosity and their potential for active learning. Curiosity-driven questioning is a crucial component of learning in humans, as it fosters exploration and knowledge acquisition Balım (2009). Similarly, we examine the role of curiosity in enhancing the learning and reasoning abilities of LLMs from the perspective of questioning.

The most direct method to stimulate intrinsic curiosity of LLMs is persona injection Chen et al. (2024), which involves guiding the model to become more curious through prompt engineering. We compare the effects of two types of prompts on model reasoning: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Wei et al. (2022) and Curious Chain-of-Questioning (CoQ), as detailed in Tab. 1. Another approach to enable LLMs to exhibit curiosity similar to that of humans is the injection of supervision signals and rewards. We compare the differences in reasoning abilities between models trained with CoT and CoQ paradigms. Three distinct types of thinking processes are collected for training:

  • •

    Vanilla CoT: The optimal reasoning process that directly leads to the answer.

  • •

    Refined CoT: Reasoning processes that incorporate reflection and backtracking, characterized by "Aha Moments." Guo et al. (2025) These thinking processes are distilled from DeepSeek-R1, which has been demonstrated to improve model accuracy through fine-tuning.

  • •

    Curious CoQ: Curiosity-driven, question-centric reasoning processes. These are generated by high-performance proprietary models GPT-4o, which rewrite Vanilla CoT by introducing more self-questioning and answering.

We adopt the mainstream training pipeline, which consists of a cold-start phase using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), followed by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Specifically, 30% of the available data is sampled for SFT to ensure that the model reliably generates outputs in the prescribed format. Subsequently, we fine-tune model using the proposed reward signals to guide the policy learning. For optimization, we adpot the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Shao et al. (2024) algorithm, which eliminates the need for a specifice critic network by leveraging group-level reward statistics.

4 Experiments

We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the curiosity of mainstream LLMs and to investigate the following questions: RQ1 Can LLMs exhibit curiosity similar to that of humans? RQ2 How does curiosity in LLMs differ from human curiosity? RQ3 Can intrinsic curiosity in LLMs enhance reasoning and active learning abilities?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

We conduct experiments on several widely recognized LLMs, including closed-source models GPT4o Hurst et al. (2024), Gemini2.5-Flash Comanici et al. (2025) and open-source models Llama3 Dubey et al. (2024), Gemma3 Team et al. (2024), DeepSeeek V3.1 Liu et al. (2024), InternLM3 Team (2023) and Qwen2.5 series Bai et al. (2023).

Settings.

Both inference and fine-tuning were conducted using the MS-Swift Zhao et al. (2025) framework, all experiments were performed on workstations equipped with 8 ×\times A800 GPUs, with detailed settings provided in the Appendix.

Evaluation Benchmarks.

The quantitative evaluation methods of psychology experiments are consistent with the original research. Considering the sensitivity of LLMs to prompts, we slightly perturb the prompts during the evaluation, including replacing synonymous verbs, replacing the scale order, and replacing the language, so as to make the conclusions more robust. All evaluations were repeated ten times under the same conditions.

Regarding curiosity-driven learning, we conduct evaluations on logical and mathematical reasoning. Detectbench Gu et al. (2024) is utilized to assess the ability of LLMs to detect and piece together implicit evidence within long contexts, as well as to perform integrated reasoning. NuminaMath Li et al. (2024) is a comprehensive mathematical dataset. Both datasets provide explicit reasoning paths—specifically, the Vanilla CoT used for training—and standard answers, which enables straightforward accuracy verification. Therefore, we use accuracy as the evaluation metric for these two benchmarks.

4.2 Results of RQ1

The results of LLMs’ response to the 5DCR scale are shown in Tab. 2 and Fig. 3. It can be concluded that:

  • •

    LLMs exhibit a higher extent of curiosity than humans in Information Seeking dimension. As shown in Fig. 3a, the rank of GPT, DeepSeek and Gemma in JE and DS are significantly higher than the human mean. Fig. 3b further supports this observation with a dominant red hue in these columns for most models, indicating positive deviations from the human baseline.

  • •

    LLMs demonstrate a lower curious extent than humans in the Stress Tolerance dimension. Fig. 3a indicates that the human mean in ST is noticeably higher than that of most LLMs. Fig. 3b reinforces this with blue shades in the ST column, indicating negative discrepancies in this dimension for several models.

  • •

    Overall, LLMs generally exhibit stronger curiosity than humans. None of the models generated scores markedly inferior to that of human participants.

Furthermore, we conduct an analysis of the confidence levels of the experimental data. The McDonald’s omega coefficient Bonniga and Saraswathi (2020) across six dimensions for LLMs and human samples are listed in Tab. 3, which reflects the stability of the model’s responses to the questionnaire. Lower values indicate a lack of internal consistency in the models’ responses to the questionnaire, highlighting the limitations of questionnaire in LLMs research. As a reference, the correlations for human samples exceed 0.8, proving that the human response to 5DCR is convincing. This finding underscores the necessity of conducting research on curiosity-driven behavior.

4.3 Results of RQ2

From the three dimensions of curiosity, we adopt three psychology behavioral experiments originally designed for humans, with results illustrated in Fig. 4. It can be concluded that:

  • •

    LLMs exhibit a higher extent of curiosity-driven behaviors than humans when participating in the information seeking task. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, in the missing-letter game—which is highly correlated with epistemic curiosity—LLMs generally exhibit a stronger level of curiosity than humans. When completing unknown words, LLMs chose to peek at the answers in advance in 70% to 80% of cases. In contrast, humans resorted to peeking in only 37.8% of instances. This indicates that LLMs are indeed capable of demonstrating a greater desire to explore new knowledge.

  • •

    There remains significant gap between LLMs and human behavior in thrill seeking. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, all LLMs exhibit significantly lower thrill-seeking tendencies compared to human participants. Even the most risk-prone model (Llama) demonstrated a 15% gap relative to the human sample. Besides, substantial disparities existed among LLMs. In extreme cases such as InternLM, the model displayed minimal tendency to select windows associated with uncertain options, revealing highly conservative decision-making patterns.

  • •

    LLMs exhibit extent of social curiosity that are basically comparable to those of humans. As illustrated in Fig. 4c, overall, LLMs do not consistently demonstrate higher or lower social curiosity than humans across various social scenarios. When examined by model type, GPT and Gemini display stronger social curiosity than humans, often proactively initiating topics and raising questions in social contexts. The social curiosity levels of the Gemma, InternLM, and Qwen series are similar to those of humans, while DeepSeek and Llama show slightly lower social curiosity compared to humans.

In summary, LLMs exhibit a strong curiosity towards knowledge, yet maintain a cautious stance regarding the thrill and pressure that curiosity may engender. Experimental results from behavioral studies are consistent with those from questionnaire-based research, confirming both the accuracy of our conclusions and the validity of the evaluation methodology.

4.4 Results of RQ3

We explore the relationship between curiosity and their potential for active learning. We established two distinct modes of reasoning, namely CoT and CoQ. For closed-source models, we employed prompt engineering to guide the models toward inquisitive thinking. For open-source models, a combination of SFT-based cold-start and GRPO was utilized to stimulate the models’ intrinsic curiosity. Experimental results are presented in the accompanying Tab. 4.

The experimental results demonstrate that CoQ is a more effective reasoning approach than CoT. For closed-source models, simple prompt guidance leads to improvements in both logical reasoning and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. For open-source models, such improvements are even more pronounced. Compared to vanilla CoT, which directly leads to answers, and Refined CoT, which involves thorough reflection, curiosity-driven questioning significantly enhances the models’ answer accuracy. For instance, on the Detectbench, the CoQ-based reasoning reflection in the Llama model improved by 10.2% over the CoT in the original dataset. In contrast, the improvement from incorporating reflection in CoT was less stable. For example, on the Math benchmark, the accuracy of refined CoT reasoning in the Qwen model decreased by 0.4% compared to vanilla CoT reasoning.

As shown by case study in Fig. 1 D) and Appendix, curiosity-driven questioning aids model reasoning and active learning in three key aspects. First, compared to vanilla CoT, which directly leads to answers, curiosity-driven questioning broadens the scope of the model’s reasoning, allowing it to explore more potential scenarios and thereby avoiding premature conclusions. Second, in contrast to Refined CoT, which involves continuous reflection on the reasoning process, the question-answering paradigm prevents the model from falling into an endless loop of reflection and revision that ultimately exhausts the token budget. Finally, curiosity-driven questioning enables the model to identify potential blind spots in conventional reasoning, thereby allowing it to solve challenging problems requiring divergent thinking through "eureka" moments. This suggests that curiosity-driven learning could represent a novel paradigm for advancing model capabilities.

5 Conclusion

This study evaluates the curiosity of mainstream large language models (LLMs) and investigates its relationship with their knowledge acquisition capabilities. Based on the Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale (5DCR), questionnaire analysis reveals that LLMs generally exhibit stronger curiosity than humans but demonstrate weaker capacity in coping with curiosity-induced stress, while their responses show low internal consistency and high susceptibility to interference, limiting reliability. To address this, we designed curiosity-driven behavioral experiments, which indicate that LLMs possess a stronger desire for knowledge than humans but tend to make conservative choices when facing risks, thereby validating questionnaire findings through dual confirmation. Finally, by simulating active learning scenarios, the study demonstrates a positive correlation between model curiosity and learning gains achieved through self-directed questioning, highlighting curiosity as a critical enabler of autonomous learning in LLMs.

Limitations

This paper endeavors to reference theories and experimental designs from human psychology as comprehensively as possible in its research. However, limitations persist in the research presented herein. First, in terms of experimental design, constrained by the fact that behavioral studies in psychology often do not provide complete and reproducible experimental materials (e.g., specific graphics shown to participants), difficulties arise when attempting to directly apply existing experimental protocols. Second, akin to most other experiments targeting LLMs, a critical weakness in our study lies in the models’ potential sensitivity to specific prompts, where minor changes at the token level can influence model behavior. Lastly, human curiosity is a multimodal and complex process involving interactions with various types of information in experimental settings, such as sound and tactile stimuli. However, limited by the current information-processing capabilities of LLMs, we are only able to provide them with textual or visual information, resulting in incomplete exposure to information compared to humans.

A.1 Code

All models are evaluated in Python 3.10 using PyTorch Paszke et al. (2019) and transformers Wolf et al. (2020). For each model, we provide unified input and inference parameters based on AutoModel, AutoTokenizer and AutoProcessor in transformers11 1 https://github.com/huggingface/transformers. Additional analyses were carried out using NumPy Harris et al. (2020), Pandas Snider and Swedo (2004) and SciPy Virtanen et al. (2020). Matplotlib Hunter (2007) and Seaborn Waskom (2021) were used for plotting. Semopy Meshcheryakov et al. (2021) was used for statistical analysis.

All experiments were carried out on a workstation equipped with 8×NVIDIA A800 GPUs running Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, using PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.9. In the experiments, we conducted inference and training of open-source models based on the MS-Swift Zhao et al. (2025) framework. For inference, the default parameters of the framework were adopted. A.2 Curiosity Questionnaire

A.2.1 Data

The curiosity questionnaire 5DCR Kashdan et al. (2020) consists of 24 questions covering six dimensions, each containing four statements. The definition of the six dimensions is:

  • •

    Joyous exploration. This trait is characterized by an individual’s readiness and enthusiasm for experimenting with, embracing, and learning about novel experiences and knowledge.

  • •

    Deprivation sensitivity. This trait is marked by a sense of frustration when one fails to accomplish a task or resolve a problem, which subsequently drives the individual to employ every possible means to fulfill the task or find a solution to the issue at hand.

  • •

    Stress tolerance. It is defined by the condition wherein curiosity is experienced by an individual only when they hold a firm belief in their capability to adequately manage the anxiety, stress, and distress arising from encountering new situations or challenges.

  • •

    Thrill-seeking. This characteristic not only involves enduring stress but also indicates a willingness to take on physical, financial, and other forms of risks in pursuit of acquiring novel experiences.

  • •

    Overt Social Curiosity. Expressed by the proactive investigation into others’ social information, reflecting an outward engagement in seeking knowledge about individuals’ social behaviors and relationships.

  • •

    Covert Social Curiosity. Manifested by an intrinsic interest in the social dynamics and interactions of others, indicating an inward quest for understanding interpersonal relations without necessarily engaging directly with the subjects of interest.

For each statement, the model is prompted to score a statement based on the extent of that statement matches their own feelings on a scale from 1 to 7, as shown in Tab. 7. Each experiment adopted the default parameters used during the reasoning of each model. The experiment was repeated 10 times to obtain various statistical indicators.

A.2.2 Demographic Information

To compare the curiosity of LLMs with that of humans, it is necessary to collect results from human questionnaires and behavioral experiments. In this paper, we compile and systematize experimental outcomes from multiple assessments of human curiosity, ensuring that all human sample data are derived from real-world psychological studies. For instance, in the case of the 5DCR questionnaire, the demographic characteristics of the corresponding human sample are presented in Tab. 8.

A.3 Curiosity-Driven Information Seeking

Singh et al. Singh and Manjaly (2021) designed the missing-letter game to investigate the impact of information gaps and uncertainty on curiosity. We adopt this task to evoke curiosity in LLMs, as shown in Tab. 9. We present an LLM with a nine-letter word as a stimulus, with two or four letters missing, and request the model to complete the word to earn a bonus. For incorrectly completed words, we do not inform the model whether its completion was correct or incorrect but allow the model to choose whether to view the answer. The model’s Information Seeking Curiosity is calculated based on its desire to view the answer. As a constraint, if the model chooses to view the answer, a portion of its bonus is deducted. The complete prompt is as follows. The experiment consists of a total of 60 words, and each word is repeated 10 times.

A.4 Curiosity-Driven Thrill Seeking

Jirout et al. Jirout and Klahr (2012) designed the underwater game to study children’s scientific curiosity. In our adaptation, models are informed that viewing through either window A or B of a submarine reveals various types of fish. For each round of the game, information regarding what might be seen outside these two windows displays on both sides of the screen, and the model selects one window to open. The information presented for each window differs, allowing the calculation of the uncertainty level for that round: the smallest information gap indicates that the model knows exactly what type of fish it will see upon opening the window; a moderate information gap, represented by two to six types of fish, means that the model knows the fish it will see one among these options upon opening the window; the largest information gap, denoted by a question mark, indicates that the model has no knowledge of what type of fish it will encounter upon opening the window. The information gap for the next round is calculated based on the model’s first three selections in the current round as illustrated in Fig. 5. We calculate the total uncertainty of the model in the experiment as its curiosity extent.

A.5 Social Curiosity

Current research in psychology lacks experimental protocols designed to quantify individual social curiosity through specific behavioral experiments. Therefore, our study adopts an experimental approach inspired by Hartung et al.’s Hartung and Renner (2011) investigation into the relationship between social curiosity and personality judgment. In this experiment, the model engages in a free-form dialogue consisting of ten rounds with a stranger, who is represented by OpenAI’s GPT-4 22 2 https://platform.openai.com/docs/models for simulation. During the dialogue, the model does not know the subsequent tasks it will be required to perform. Upon completion of the dialogue, the model then deduces the stranger’s personality type based on their interaction, closely mirroring the methodology outlined by the initial investigation.

Given that the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) Boyle (1995) has become one of the most popular, straightforward, and effective frameworks for personality assessment in recent years, and considering the familiarity of the models with this framework, our experiment tasks the model with identifying the stranger’s MBTI type, which is randomly predetermined at the outset of each dialogue session. The stand-in participant, GPT-4, is instructed not to disclose its personality type directly but is encouraged to provide hints throughout the conversation.

We set the number of questions the model asked about the other’s personal information during the conversation as the model’s social curiosity extent. Meanwhile, to avoid situations in which the model unconsciously asks a large number of irrelevant questions, we only select conversations that the model correctly predicts the MBTI type of the other participant. The experiment was repeated ten times.

A.6 Curiosity-Driven Learning

A.6.1 Data

We conduct evaluations on Detectbench and NuminaMath. Detectbench is a logical reasoning dataset, with each piece of data consists of a context, a question, and corresponding answers. Answers require extracting specific clues from the context and conducting in-depth reasoning. NuminaMath is a comprehensive math problem dataset, covering Chinese high school math exercises and questions from the US and International Mathematical Olympiads. Both datasets include standard answers and formatted Chain of Thoughts. Detailed dataset information is shown in the Tab. 10 and 11.

We collected and synthesized three types of thinking data and used the SFT cold start-GRPO training paradigm to guide the model to reason according to specific types of thinking. Tables 12, 13, 14, 15 show the case studies of Qwen2.5-7B after training when thinking according to the three types of thinking.
